Both readers describe problem -> vocabulary -> table -> alternatives and scale -> applied case -> failures, matching problem_solution with prerequisite_order; no section is unclear to either. Reader B's point that scale stages are used before their section is not counted: the stages are in audience.already_knows.

results.quote: The scene used "record" and "copy" without defining them.
results.finding: The introduction already defined a system of record, so this sentence reads as a contradiction and the second, fuller definition in ¶3 makes readers check whether the meaning changed. Reader A item 1: 'I stopped there, because "record" had been defined in the opening.'
results.corroborated_by: reader-flow-b item 5 (system of record defined twice)

results.quote: Naming one gives support and other systems a place to resolve disagreements.
results.finding: Following the parcel hook at once with the system of record steers readers to read the parcel as a stale-record problem, while the chapter later resolves it as two true statuses of different objects; and the scene that follows is about stock, not the parcel. Reader A item 2: 'I only understood what the hook meant when I reached the Three-Status Order.' The spec's bridge frames the parcel as an authority problem and its callback as a bounded-context one, so the fault may lie in the spec as well as the prose.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flow-b item 10 (hook about an order, scene about stock; unsure how the parcel related until Bounded Contexts)

results.finding: Opens with a puzzling scenario (the parcel), not a placeholder, restated question, definition, 'dawn of man' or book report.

The author's synthesis states what no section states (write the table before buying a hub; a bought OMS fed by unreconciled sources is a fifth copy; a table without reconciliation is a record on trust) and why it matters.
Returns to the parcel: 'neither status was stale, each was true of its own object, and what was missing was an owner of the view across them.'

Reader predicted records and copies, the meanings of 'order', the entity–owner table, a comparison of ownership choices with vendor documentation, and Kestrel & Pine's stock before and after Waypoint, in order.
Reader asks first which system is the record and second who can write the value in the record and each copy, and rejects syncing faster.
Reader says all three are right because each 'order' is a different object in its own bounded context, and names the missing owner of the cross-context view (the OMS).
Reader fills record, writers, copies, how copies learn (event, exact at promotion boundaries) and how disagreement is found (hourly per-channel comparison), all specific.
